sections.summary: The neutral reading identifies Paul's use of the peri de formula to introduce the Corinthians' question about pneumatika ('spiritual things' or 'spiritual persons'), which Paul will answer on entirely different terms than the Corinthians asked, reframing the question from spiritual ranking to the character of grace-gifts.

sections.section_title: The Criterion: From Mute Idols to the Confession of the Lord
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the contrast between the Corinthians' former passive captivity under pagan ecstasy and the present criterion for genuine Spirit-activity — the confession 'Jesus is Lord' — which the neutral reading identifies as a democratizing principle establishing that every genuine member of the community has the Spirit, eliminating any division between Spirit-haves and Spirit-have-nots.

sections.section_title: One Source, Three Dimensions of Diversity
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the three-fold pattern of diverse gifts from the same Spirit, diverse services under the same Lord, and diverse activities empowered by the same God as establishing that the community's diversity of function flows from the unity of its divine source, making division a contradiction of the community's own origin.

sections.section_title: The Purpose of Manifestation: The Common Good
sections.summary: The neutral reading identifies that every member receives a manifestation of the Spirit, given universally and without exception, and that the purpose of every manifestation is the common benefit (pros to sympheron) rather than private display or status enhancement.

The neutral reading presents the catalog of nine gifts — word of wisdom, word of knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment of spirits, tongues, and interpretation — as illustrative examples of the principle of diversity, noting that Paul subordinates the Corinthians' most prized categories (wisdom, knowledge) to the Spirit's distribution and places tongues last as a deliberate corrective to Corinthian ranking.

The neutral reading presents the Spirit as the single source who works all the gifts and who distributes them 'to each one individually as he wills,' locating the decision about which gift each member receives in the Spirit's own deliberate purpose rather than in human merit, effort, or spiritual superiority.

sections.section_title: The Body Metaphor Introduced: Baptism into One Body
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the community as one body constituted through baptism in one Spirit, transcending the divisions of Jew and Greek, slave and free, with the shared experience of drinking of one Spirit paralleling Israel's drinking from the spiritual Rock in the wilderness.
sections.relevance: The neutral reading explicitly draws the typological parallel between the community's Spirit-baptism and Spirit-drinking and Israel's baptism into Moses and drinking in the wilderness (10:1-4), and then states the implication directly: 'Receiving the Spirit, like receiving the manna and the water, does not automatically guarantee perseverance.' The chapter summary reinforces this: 'Universal participation in divine gifts — whether Israel's baptism, food, and drink, or the community's baptism and Spirit-drinking — does not automatically prevent judgment. The body must be discerned. The gifts must be used for the common good. The members must care for one another.' This presents ongoing human response — discerning, exercising gifts rightly, caring for one another — as necessary for the salvific benefit of Spirit-reception to hold, rather than treating Spirit-reception as a divine guarantee of final outcome. However, the text itself is addressing the constitution of the body rather than directly stating who determines salvation, and the warning about perseverance is drawn from the parallel to chapter 10 rather than from an explicit statement within 12:12-13 itself.
key_phrases: in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body
all were made to drink of one Spirit
Receiving the Spirit, like receiving the manna and the water, does not automatically guarantee perseverance

sections.section_title: The Body Cannot Reject Its Own Members
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Paul's argument that diversity is constitutive of the body's existence — a body of one member is not a body — with God as the one who arranged the members as he chose, addressing members who self-exclude because they lack the spectacular gifts and assuring them that belonging is determined by baptism, not by which gift one has.

sections.section_title: The Body Cannot Despise Its Own Members
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents Paul's argument that no member can claim self-sufficiency or dismiss others as expendable, with God's deliberate counter-hierarchical composition of the body giving greater honor to the parts that lack it, designed to prevent division and produce mutual care where suffering and honor are shared communally.

The neutral reading presents the shift from metaphor to direct declaration — 'you are the body of Christ and individually members of it' — identifying the community as the visible, tangible presence of Christ in Corinth, with corporate identity and individual distinctiveness held together without resolving in favor of one over the other.

The neutral reading presents God as the one who appointed roles in the assembly with an explicit functional ordering — first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, healing, helping, administrating, and tongues last — with tongues' consistent placement at the bottom of every list serving as deliberate correction to Corinthian ranking.

sections.section_title: The Rhetorical Questions: Diversity Is Essential
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents seven rhetorical questions, each expecting the answer 'no,' making the principle of diversity inescapable: not all are apostles, not all prophets, not all tongues-speakers, forcing the community to acknowledge that the absence of any particular gift is by God's design, not a deficiency.

sections.section_title: The Transition: Earnest Desire and a More Excellent Way
sections.summary: The neutral reading presents the transition from the gifts discourse to the way of love, with Paul either acknowledging or commanding the pursuit of the greater gifts while pointing beyond gifts altogether to love as the governing disposition for all gift-exercise, preventing chapter 12 from being read as self-contained.
